Toyota expands C-HR EV recall to 19,000 globally

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (479 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Toyota is recalling 19,000 electric C-HR SUVs globally, with about 10,000 affected in the US.
  • In September, Toyota issued a safety recall involving certain model-year 2026 C-HR electric SUVs in North America.
  • Toyota initially said about 10,000 models were involved, but later confirmed the number was 8,521 in a letter to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota is recalling 19,000 electric C-HR SUVs globally, with about 10,000 affected in the US.

In September, Toyota issued a safety recall involving certain model-year 2026 C-HR electric SUVs in North America.

Toyota initially said about 10,000 models were involved, but later confirmed the number was 8,521 in a letter to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).

Recent findings suggest that according to Germany’s federal motor authority, Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the recall has now expanded to 19,000 C-HR vehicles globally. In Germany, the recall impacts 1,096 vehicles and is still under investigation by the KBA.

The glitch stems from faulty software programming in the EV-ECU. While it’s intended to limit the battery’s charge level, the software can cause it to overcharge under certain conditions.

Toyota said the glitch occurs if the battery is already at a high state of charge and the driver continues using the regenerative braking system.

When this happens, warning lights and a sound will alert the driver, and the electric drive system can shut down, causing the vehicle to lose power while driving.

Following an internal investigation, Toyota mentioned in the NHTSA report that the concern was caused by incorrect software that disrupted the charging-limit function, allowing the battery to overcharge while driving.

The Toyota C-HR vehicles included in the recall were produced between June 17, 2025, and July 9, 2026.

In Europe and other overseas markets, Toyota sells the C-HR EV as the C-HR+ to distinguish it from the gas- or hybrid-powered version.

Industry observers note that OTA would be great, but there are some systems that are isolated and can't be updated that way. The EV-ECU is a core function system that is very likely sealed to prevent tampering. They never expected to need to reprogram it. It's like the firmware on your phone.

Owners of affected vehicles in North America can take them to a Toyota dealership, where the battery ECU software will be updated free of charge.

Toyota mailed owner notification letters out on October 18, 2026. Owners can contact Toyota’s customer service at 1-800-331-4331. The recall number is 26TA17.

Other than saying the EV-ECU is being reprogrammed, Toyota has not yet confirmed next steps for owners of affected vehicles outside North America. The KBA reference number is 17116R.

According to recent reports, check back for more details. The recall only affects the 2026 C-HR. The 2027 Toyota C-HR is also now on sale.

Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

📅 01 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1376 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated initiative of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.
  • The reports detail how cardiovascular health challenges can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.
  • The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated initiative of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health challenges can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

They stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

The authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” said Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”.

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, said the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she said.

“I am incredibly excited to see these new reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah said.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”.

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg said this life-stage breakdown is important, especially for risk reduction.

She said issues with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg remarked.

Suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”.

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” noted Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive strategy for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”.

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

“These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”.

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are vital windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” said William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”.

Recent findings suggest that the authors note several age-related warning signs of heart challenges. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

Females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” noted Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”.

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

It has been revealed that the organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

The authors of that report listed several steps they stated could reverse these trends. Among them:.

Experts say women can also take action on their own to reduce their risks. Suppogu suggests the following:.

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She mentioned that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

Khan mentioned women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

“Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”.

It has been revealed that you don't need much of an imagination to picture yourself curled up on one of 7th Avenue's sectionals. One look at the extra deep seats and plush cushions is enough to have you planning your movie marathon—pass the popcorn, please. But even so, a couch is the sort of thing you want to try before you buy. With the opening of a new flagship showroom in New York City's SoHo neighborhood, the brand is hoping you'll make a day of it; get comfortable, stay a while.

Sources indicate that this month, 7th Avenue cut the ribbon on a 3,240-square-foot storefront in a historic cast-iron building at 476 Broome Street. It's the 30th brick-and-mortar space in the US and first permanent location in NYC to open since the brand's founding as a direct-to-consumer business in 2022. Co-founder and CEO Billy Shaw notes that he and co-founder Josh Stinson decided to put down roots in the Big Apple after seeing the way New Yorkers took to their hero product—the "World's Greatest Modular Sofa," they call it—during the years they operated a pop-up shop in the city.

“The main showroom celebrates volume and openness, with soaring ceilings, dramatic columns, and refined architectural detailing,” claims Stinson.

Co-founders Stinson and Shaw sourced design details for the showroom from around the world. “[These items] have an Old-World patina that balances the modern, contemporary aesthetics of our sofas,” states Shaw.

"We were inspired to create 7th Avenue to solve for a frustration we kept hearing from customers: Finding a sofa that was both beautifully designed and genuinely practical for everyday living was surprisingly difficult," Shaw claims. (The brand famously uses water-repellent and stain-resistant performance fabrics, and all sofa covers can be removed and thrown in the washing machine for cleaning.) New Yorkers appreciated the modular designs, which can fit into petite elevators and through the narrow doors and hallways ubiquitous in city homes (gotta love a pre-war building!). “Our sofas arrive in individual boxes, making those tight spaces easier to navigate,” he adds.

A store in Latest York was a no-brainer, but that doesn't mean finding a location was easy. Shaw and Stinson, who is COO, considered addresses in the Flatiron District, where shoppers can bop in and out of home retailers—like Herman Miller, Design Within Reach, ABC Carpet & Home, Crate & Barrel, the list goes on—without leaving a three-block radius. But ultimately they couldn't let go of SoHo's "unmatched" energy. "We wanted to find a place that is grand and historic, paying homage to NYC’s architectural heritage," says Stinson. With 14-foot ceilings and a skylight, "the space on Broome Street creates a sense of openness and grandeur from the moment customers walk through the door.".

In a recent development, just how durable are 7th Avenue's furniture pieces? During the SoHo store's opening party, guests were encouraged to drop their drinks on the sofas in a “spill lab.”.

Shaw and Stinson, who designed the space themselves, say they used the building's architecture to create different vignettes and experiences for guests. The main showroom, for instance, with its dramatic columns and open space, is perfect for showing off 7th Avenue's larger sectionals. Elsewhere, a daybed is nestled into an alcove for a more intimate scene. "We wanted to demonstrate that great furniture design isn't simply about size," states Stinson. "It's about proportion and the relationship between a piece and the space surrounding it.".

The two also wanted to show that "beautiful design should work for real life." "That meant balancing the stateliness of the cast-iron architecture and high ceilings with warm materials, organic textures, and comfortable places to sit," indicates Shaw.

Sources indicate that A light and bright backdrop of European oak and Turkish travertine is dotted with treasures gathered from around the world: coral stone coffee tables quarried from volcanic islands in Indonesia, century-old olive oil jars from Turkey and Morocco, sculptural plants like a Hawaiian dragon tree. "A Queensland Bottle Tree Bonsai, native to Australia and sourced from Los Angeles plant specialists The Plant Daddies, was shaped over two years to achieve its distinctive curved form," says Stinson. These details, Shaw adds, have "an Old-World patina that balances the modern, contemporary aesthetics of our sofas.".

Guests readily settled into 7th Avenue's plush sofas at the flagship's opening party.

It has been revealed that "We want customers to feel comfortable settling into this beautiful sofa, yet imagining it in their own home and being used in their day-to-day lives," says Stinson. At the opening party, props scattered about the furniture brought this idea to life.

Industry observers note that for all the finery, 476 Broome Street feels more like someone's home than an art gallery—and that's very on purpose. "We want customers to feel comfortable settling into this beautiful sofa, yet imagining it in their own home and being used in their day-to-day lives," says Stinson. The co-founders want visitors to interact with the furniture. Indeed, a cheeky neon sign that reads "Come Spill on Me" hangs over an emerald velvet couch; at the store's opening party, red wine was passed with nonchalance and guests were invited to plop onto a double-wide sofa and pose for photos with an artful disarray of newspapers, a pizza box, and an overturned gag martini glass—no need to take their shoes off.

According to Shaw and Stinson, great design should accommodate the realities of modern life, messy things like kids, pets, and parties. "Our clients appreciate beautiful, thoughtfully designed spaces, but they also want to live in them without hesitation," states Shaw. "Ultimately, we feel that luxury should be lived in, not simply admired.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US has installed more than 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage, with nearly 50 GWh coming online in the first nine months of 2026 alone.
  • The US added 48.3 GWh of battery storage through September, up 20% from the same stretch last year, according to the latest report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.
  • Texas added 12.3 GWh of grid-scale batteries through September, more than any other state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US has installed more than 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage, with nearly 50 GWh coming online in the first nine months of 2026 alone.

The US added 48.3 GWh of battery storage through September, up 20% from the same stretch last year, according to the latest report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Q3 was a little slower: The US installed 14.3 GWh in those three months, down 1% year over year.

Texas added 12.3 GWh of grid-scale batteries through September, more than any other state. Arizona came in second at 7.7 GWh, followed by California at 6.8 GWh. And 11 states had already broken their annual storage installation records with three months to go – Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois.

In a recent development, utility-scale batteries did most of the work in Q3, accounting for 12.2 GWh of new capacity. Businesses and industrial sites added another 1.3 GWh, and residential added 746 megawatt-hours (MWh). That was the best Q3 yet for home batteries, though installs through September were still down 12% year over year. Some homeowners moved up their installations last year before the federal residential clean energy tax credit ended.

In a recent development, “States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” remarked Pete Tillotson, a senior analyst at Benchmark. In September, New York awarded contracts for eight battery projects that can deliver about 950 megawatts (MW) combined. SEIA and Benchmark now expect 708 GWh of storage across the grid, homes, and businesses by 2030, up 3.7% from their previous forecast.

The US can also make more battery cells here. A Tennessee factory opened in July and an Indiana factory opened in October, bringing US cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, up 50%.

Solar and batteries helped bring down average summer wholesale power prices by 42% in Texas’s ERCOT market and 51% in California’s CAISO market between 2021 and 2026, according to SEIA’s inflation-adjusted analysis. When batteries had power to spare during peak hours, grid operators could call on expensive power plants less often.

You wouldn’t know it from looking at the total on residential electric bills. The cost of generating power for households fell in both markets, but the cost of delivering it to homes rose. Overall, residential bills rose 22% at the two California utilities SEIA examined and 3% across its Texas utility sample, driven by higher transmission and distribution costs. California is upgrading its grid to reduce the risk of wildfires. Texas is expanding its grid for rising demand and make it more resilient to storms.

The article is good with the reporting about grid tied storage, but seems to miss the forest for the trees with it comes to pricing. Texas isn't installing more grid tied storage because of altruistic intent.

In a recent development, the storage is being added because they electricity suppliers can use it to make money. They can make money because we have a reasonably well thought out wholesale electrical market AND because that market has purchases large amounts of solar and wind generation.

That combination means that I still pay just $0.01 more per kwh than I did when I moved to this state 20 years ago. I pay 12 cents per kwh and Texas average is between 12 and 15. A functional market is what makes that work.

More than 300 solar and battery storage companies in the US wrote to Congress last week asking it to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty indicates the permitting bill would help get projects built faster and ease pressure on power prices. However, many Democrats feel this bill falls short. The Senate voted 70–27 on Monday to end debate on the amendment containing the bill’s text, moving it closer to a final vote.

#109891. Experts Say Weightlifting Is the Fountain of Youth. Here's How to Get Started at Any Age

📅 19 Nov 2024 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1976 w)

Experts Say Weightlifting Is the Fountain of Youth. Here's How to Get Started at Any Age

📅 19 Nov 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you want to age independently—haul your own groceries, get up stairs, and play with your grandkids)—here’s the science-backed secret: lift weights.
  • According to recent reports, getting older doesn’t have to mean getting weaker.
  • Recent findings suggest that women start losing muscle after 30, and this speeds up after menopause due to dramatic changes in your hormone levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you want to age independently—haul your own groceries, get up stairs, and play with your grandkids)—here’s the science-backed secret: lift weights. Yep, those dumbbells in the gym aren’t just for young buffs (you know this!)—and they’re your ticket to keep doing the things you love most.

According to recent reports, getting older doesn’t have to mean getting weaker. In fact, senior weight lifting—doing resistance training with machines and/or free weights in your 60s and beyond—offers physical and mental benefits that make it a vital part of aging well.

Recent findings suggest that women start losing muscle after 30, and this speeds up after menopause due to dramatic changes in your hormone levels. This change impacts both muscle and bone health, but strength training can help maintain bone density, promote preservation (and even addition!) of muscle, and set your body up for an active, independent life, according to the International Osteoporosis Foundation.

Here, we share all the fundamentals you need to understand why weight lifting and strength training are so vital as you age, and how you can (safely!) get started.

Aging gracefully isn't just about staying active; it’s about choosing the right kind of activity to support your health. Resistance training (with bodyweight, free weight, and resistance band exercises) is one of the best ways to counter the effects of aging, helping you build up muscle to support daily activities and prevent conditions like osteopenia and osteoporosis that can lead to bone fractures. And even if you've never lifted a weight before, it's never too late to start.

“Weight training is the fountain of youth,” states Abby Bales, PT, DPT, CSCS, founder of Reform Physical Therapy. “Not only does it help increase and maintain bone density to prevent fractures, but the muscle mass that weight training builds also helps to regulate our blood sugar and metabolism.” Weight lifting can even improve balance and coordination, decreasing the frequency, severity, and likelihood of falls.

Industry observers note that want to gain serious strength? Try our Strong After 50 4-Week workout proposal.

On top of the physical benefits, resistance training has shown promise in staving off neurological conditions like Alzheimer’s and dementia, according to a 2023 study published in Frontiers in Neuroscience, making it a multi-benefit tool for aging well. You can think of lifting weights as your body’s best tool to promote resilience, energy, and independence through the aging process.

Starting with small, manageable steps—such as incorporating resistance bands or light weights into your routine—can help you gain confidence and momentum while reaping the long-term benefits.

The best exercises for women over 60 are weight-bearing and promote strength, posture, and/or balance (sometimes all at once!). While the best exercises for each individual depend on factors including medical history, fitness level, and personal preference (a personal trainer or physical therapist can help you design a more personalized blueprint!), it’s always great to start with fundamental exercises that incorporate movements used in daily life.

To help get you started, here are a few exercises that Bales recommends older women incorporate in their weekly routine.

Instructions: Select five to seven of the exercises below, mixing two to three upper body exercises, two to three lower body, and one or two core. Start with two to three sets of 10 reps of each. If you’re new to strength training, begin by doing the routine once a week and gradually work up to three times per week. Choose a weight that feels heavy enough to make the last two to three reps of each set feel tough, yet achievable.

Time: 15 to 20 minutes | Equipment: Dumbbells, kettlebells, stair or step-up platform | Good for: Full-body.

Why it rocks: The air squat mimics many daily activities, such as getting up and down from a toilet seat, standing up from a chair, and bending down to pick something up. All of these activities are crucial as we age, so make sure you’re doing some form of squatting as you get older to help stay independent and capable of all these tasks and more. This move is also great because it can be done using your body weight alone, although adding a weight to up the intensity is always encouraged.

Recent findings suggest that pro tip: If getting down low enough or balancing feels too challenging, try doing this with a chair or couch behind you. At the bottom of the move, tap your bum to the seat or briefly pause there before standing back up.

Why it rocks: This exercise helps with strength and mobility in the shoulder joint, which will allow you to reach items in upper cabinets or even put on/take off a T-shirt for years to come.

In a recent development, why it rocks: As we age, simple things like stepping up onto a curb, walking on uneven surfaces and going up and down stairs can become challenging and increase the risk of tripping or falling. For this reason, it’s important to practice fully picking up the feet and clearing them from the floor. This exercise focuses on just that.

In a recent development, pro tip: If this is challenging, start by doing it somewhere that you can hold onto a railing or fixed surface with one hand for support. You can also start with a low step or platform—something that’s six inches high or less—and eventually increase the height as the move becomes easier.

In a recent development, why it rocks: Your biceps help you bend your arm and make it possible to perform daily tasks such as doing your laundry, lifting a heavy pot or pan, and more. Biceps curls are a great way to keep this muscle strong.

Why it rocks: Good posture is crucial for preventing things like stress fractures, which can occur in women with low bone density due to osteoporosis. This move targets the shoulders, upper back, and biceps all at once, helping to improve posture and strength.

According to recent reports, pro tip: If you’re struggling to hinge forward, try doing it one arm at a time, and use the other arm to hold onto a chair or railing to support you. The more you hinge, the more you will target your back.

Why it rocks: Reverse lunges build strength in the glutes, hamstrings, and quads, while also improving balance and stability to help prevent falls as we age.

Pro tip: This can be a challenging exercise for many people because of the balance aspect, so try holding onto a stable object or countertop with one hand at first.

Why it rocks: Incline pushups are a gentler version of regular pushups, perfect for building arm, shoulder, and chest strength without straining your wrists or shoulders.

In a recent development, pro tip: Begin with a higher surface to reduce intensity and pressure on the wrists. You can even use a wall! As you improve with this move, gradually lower the incline to make your body more parallel to the floor, which will make the exercise feel more challenging.

Why it rocks: This move is truly a full-body functional exercise that is great for improving balance, strength, and mobility to help older adults get up and down from the floor.

Pro tip: This is a complex move, so it’s best to break it down into smaller parts first. Try it first without weights and start by practicing just one or two pieces of the movement before putting it all together.

Why it rocks: Your triceps are key for extending your elbow, making daily movements possible like pushing yourself up from the ground or supporting your bodyweight with your arms (like in a plank).

Why it rocks: This squat variation has all the perks of a classic squat, but widens the stance to target the inner thighs, glutes, and quads from a slightly different angle.

According to recent reports, why it rocks: The farmer’s carry prepares the core for real-life activities such as carrying heavy things by your sides. It strengthens the core by making you resist the urge to bend, improving stability and balance.

Why it rocks: This exercise recruits your abdominal muscles to maintain balance and stability. A resistance band offers an added challenge for the core and lower body.

It has been revealed that there really aren’t any exercises that are completely off-limits for older women, says Bales—as long as you’re comfortable. If an exercise causes pain, skip it. If it feels too challenging or confusing to get the hang of, try tweaking it to better suit your needs.

That mentioned, depending on your fitness level, bone density, and current mobility and stability level, high-impact, single-side, and twisting exercises should be approached with caution, and may be best left behind for certain people, she states.

Sources indicate that high-impact moves like jump squats and box jumps—while great for building up and strengthening your bones—put extra strain on joints, and therefore may not be a good idea for those who already experience joint pain or have arthritis, says Bales. If balance is an area of improvement for you, single-leg exercises are a great tool to rely on, as long as you’re using a stable platform to stabilize yourself and avoid ending up on the floor. Similarly, rotational exercises involving twisting of the spine are great for core strength and mobility, but can increase the risk of spinal compression fractures for those with advanced bone density challenges, she says.

Recent findings suggest that for beginners, it’s best to stick with slow, controlled resistance and bodyweight exercises that build strength without unnecessary strain, like bodyweight squats, resistance band work, or moderate weight lifting, says Bales. Above all, prioritize good form over the amount of weight you’re lifting, and don’t let fear stop you from getting started.

Bales’ bottom line: “Move as much as possible.” If you’re not sure which exercises are appropriate for you, consider seeing a physical therapist to get a full assessment and discuss your preferences and goals.

Recent findings suggest that building a strength training routine doesn’t have to be complicated—it just needs to be consistent. “Start small, build gradually, and stick with it,” claims Bales. She recommends starting with two or three sessions per week, focusing on five to six exercises from this list for three sets of 10 reps. Try selecting an equal number of upper body, lower body, and core exercises to keep things balanced.

Recent findings suggest that progress takes time, so be patient. “Results usually show in six to eight weeks,” Bales explains. The key is to keep showing up and enjoy the process—your future self will thank you.

Musk objected to LiDAR, pointing out its limitations. At the time it appeared to make sense. LiDAR was expensive and the performance was at a certain level. But the occasionally visionary Elon wasn't particularly visionary on that occasion or every time he repeated his stance. Truth is, Cameras were cheaper, and computer performance wasn't wasn't going to get there if all the added complexity was loading it up. So Tesla ditched RADAR and only briefly considered LiDAR. But LiDAR got better and it got a lot, lot cheaper, and anyway, Tesla's HW3 wasn't going to cut it either. HW4 looks like it may have a tough time for 99.999% safety. Thing is, eyesight can't deal with every single situation, and neither can cameras. So if you want to get as close to 100% safety as possible, these days it seems a bit silly to leave aside LiDAR. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to fresh research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported.
  • Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study.
  • The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to fresh research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, remarked Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

“By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she said.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz mentioned the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

She remarked researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”.

It has been revealed that weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he said. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

“It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy noted.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy stated. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

Wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, introduced in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham noted the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

The study showed links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also said the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

Cunningham mentioned adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so crucial,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive strategy,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:.

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.

Imagine if you could translate that cocooning feeling you get from your favorite reading chairs into your bedroom. Well, you can, thanks to wingback bed frames. The headboard shape has the same curved ‘wings’ as those high-back chairs. This time, they’re tucking you into bed rather than into your next read. The wing style dates back to the 1600s, serving the purpose of blocking drafts and providing extra warmth in those pre-central heating days.

In a recent development, when crafting your cozy bedroom, there are a few things to consider. One is upholstery. For people aiming to do everything from bed (we don’t judge), or those with little ones and pets, perhaps consider a performance fabric that can easily be treated with an upholstery cleaner, should sticky fingers or coffee stains leave their mark. Next is legs. Most wingback beds have a platform base, which helps to create a grounded look. But if you already have plenty of floor-sitting furniture, a slim leg could aid in giving your bedroom the levity it needs. Regardless, we’ve done the heavy lifting for you to spotlight seven of the best wingback bed frames for a dramatic bedscape.

Industry observers note that for those looking to go down the traditional route of a streamlined, upholstered wingback bed, Quince has you covered. The nubby bouclé adds a sense of warmth to your bedroom, while the tapered ‘wings’ cocoon you as you drift off to sleep. We particularly love the taller headboard, 42 inches to be exact, that shows off the curved edges no matter how plush your mattress may be. Quince offers white glove delivery for free, meaning that no assembly is required. A quick note, ivory upholstery may seem intimidating for those who prefer to drink their coffee in bed, but the performance fabric can easily be spot cleaned should the need arise.

Most wingback styles carry a sense of opulence and grandeur, but modern-minimalists can also embrace this look. The Emmy Bed from DWR has the signature “wings,” without the height of most tall wingback headboards. Even in the tall version, this frame is still shorter in height than any other competitor mentioned in this list. There are more than 50 upholstery fabrics up for grabs, but we’re partial to the linen-blend spruce colorway with slim, walnut-finished legs for an earthy, serene-looking sleepscape. Place two similarly stained wooden nightstands on either side to lay the foundation for your room.

Since a small bedroom only offers so much square footage to work with, that’s where storage beds come in handy. Saatva’s Cassis bed frame has a hydraulic lift mechanism to reveal a storage cavity built-into the platform bed frame. Saatva’s bed frames are sturdy McGregor’s experience, so you won’t have to worry about creaking, shifting, or fraying upholstery here. The high-quality build is designed to last years. Choose between a linen upholstery for a more relaxed look, or a velvet for a moodier vibe.

Your bed frame is among the largest pieces you’ll welcome into your space, and the dimensions could compromise how you move through your bedroom. Interior Define’s bespoke offerings are great for this reason, as you can choose from dozens of upholstery options, two sizes (queen or king), and two headboard heights (45 or 55 inches). If you’re tight on storage space, you can also add extra drawers to your frame. “I loved the idea of having built-in drawers and bonus storage in addition to the coziness of a fully upholstered bed frame,” indicates Melissa Maria, senior visuals editor, who selected the mink colorway. “My bedroom at the moment could be described as eclectic. The bed frame works well with my other existing pieces, as it’s a classic shape and a neutral color.”.

Industry observers note that castlery remains a top choice among our editors, especially for those of us furnishing contemporary spaces. Lisa Aiken, senior vice president of shopping at Condé Nast, added this bed frame to match the scale of other large items in her modern-minimalist, midcentury home. “Aesthetically, the wingback headboard is very eye-catching, providing a visually interesting form,” she notes. “Practically, the storage that this bed frame provides is substantial, especially the large full-width drawer at the foot of the bed.”.

After moving from a midcentury-modern Florida home to a historic home in Ohio, contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert was searching for a substantial bed frame to coordinate with her upcoming digs. She was drawn to the dusty lilac upholstery, and the subtle pull-out storage drawer to manage her self-described quilt addiction. “When I dress this bed to the nines with all my linens, it feels like I've snuck away to a Parisian boutique hotel,” Alpert says. “The shelter headboard creates a little alcove, which is lovely when I read in bed, and it feels like an embrace when I sleep.”.

Wingback frames are known for the turned-in sides, but this one gives more dimension to the original curved wingback design. From members-only social club Soho House’s furniture and decor line Soho Home, the Rivas Bed features an oversized, extra-tall headboard with rounded edges throughout and comes in several distinct colorways like this moody Bordeaux. Handcrafted in the UK, it’s a splurge-y pick that commands attention.

The 10 Best Hiking Backpacks, Tested by Outdoor Gear Editors

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A GOOD HIKING backpack is just as important—if not more so—as a good pair of hiking boots, hiking shoes, or any other hiking gear.
  • Finding the right backpack for you can be like shopping for the perfect mattress.
  • In a recent development, winner of this year’s “Best Upcoming All-Purpose Backpack” in the latest Men’s Health Outdoor Awards, the Kestrel LT 45 is the bag to buy if you only want to buy one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A GOOD HIKING backpack is just as important—if not more so—as a good pair of hiking boots, hiking shoes, or any other hiking gear. Whether you're venturing deep into the backcountry or exploring a local trail, your pack will be strapped to your back for an extended period of time. It needs to be reliable, comfortable, durable, and offer the right storage and organization options to suit your style of hiking. Oh, and affordability is a nice-to-have, too.

Finding the right backpack for you can be like shopping for the perfect mattress. Backpack technology isn't what it used to be when your grandpappy was hitting the trail. It's far better but also a lot more complicated. You'll need to understand frame types and nylon fabric densities and hydration system compatibilities and—well, you get the picture. It's all just a little more confusing than it needs to be. That's why our expert team put together this guide to the best hiking backpacks to help you find the perfect pack without breaking your back and the bank in the process.

In a recent development, winner of this year’s “Best Upcoming All-Purpose Backpack” in the latest Men’s Health Outdoor Awards, the Kestrel LT 45 is the bag to buy if you only want to buy one. It’s Osprey’s reimagining of the classic rucksack design. It’s rugged yet lightweight, with a 45-liter capacity that’s more than enough for most hikers on all but the longest multiday treks. I personally love the streamlined exterior that cinches down tight for maximum compression. Osprey’s AirScape back panel offers just-right cushioning, coupled with simple torso-length adjustability to fit a wide range of body shapes and sizes.

After months of testing, this has consistently proven to be my go-to pack for most hikes because everything about it just works. Plus, the price point hits the midrange sweet spot, ensuring it’s affordable enough for most, even for first-time hiking backpack buyers on a budget. Bonus: An attached rain cover is included.

In a recent development, at just 12 liters and weighing only 390 grams, this pack is designed for ultra-efficient climbs and lightning-fast summit assaults. It's the daypack you grab when most other daypacks are too much. I found the simple organizational layout—one main compartment and two zippered pockets (one internal, one external)—made wrangling my day hiking essentials a breeze. Additional gear loops at the rear provide extra space for hanging anything you might need at the ready. The just-right back padding, removable hip belt, and ventilated mesh shoulder straps were extremely comfy for tackling daily summits in the White Mountains.

It's all made from recycled, eco-friendly materials that are Bluesign certified, with a PFC-free DWR treatment. The best part? It's among the most affordable brand-name speedpacks we'd recommend this year.

Read More: How We Pack Hiking Backpacks.

It has been revealed that like every Gregory pack I've tested in the last two decades, the Paragon 60 is durable, cleverly designed, and features smart organizational options. But I'm including it here mainly because it's so dang comfy to wear. It features a widely adjustable torso length and an airy mesh back panel that breathes well thanks to a design that's 90 percent air. The hip belt is equally adjustable, too, with dynamic panels that move independently of the frame. Translation: It's the most comfortable pack I tested this year, even after hundreds of miles of hiking with fairly heavy loads.

Bonus: The PFAS-free durable water-repellent (DWR) coating on the body, bottom, and pack lining means it's more eco-friendly, too.

Read More: Best Cold-Weather Hiking Gear.

Yeti’s first foray into the hardcore hiking backpack game comes on the heels of its recent acquisition of the Mystery Ranch brand. The Skala is a deft combination of Mystery Ranch’s legendary design prowess and Yeti’s built-to-survive-anything durability. The former’s RipZip opening is the star of this pack, providing instant access to its contents with a quick one-handed pull. The Skala features multiple adjustment points and a clever load distribution system that combine to ensure a perfect fit and all-day comfort on the trail.

In a recent development, true to the Yeti brand, it's packed with premium, heavy-duty materials built to survive years of abuse. The only downsides? At 3.4 pounds, it’s heavier than many in this weight class. It’s also pricier than most of its competition. But if you’re a fan of Yeti and/or MR and don’t mind the “buy once, cry once” price point, this is definitely worth considering.

Read More: Yeti Skala Backpack Review.

For an all-in-one solution—a backpack that moves effortlessly from your morning commute to the office to the trail and back again—Peak Design's new Outdoor 25L pack delivers. The frameless, low-profile build is extremely comfy on and off the trail. The brand's signature organizational elements are here, too—it's hydration system-compatible, features a 16-inch laptop sleeve, and is purpose-built to accept PD's own gear cubes (sold separately) so you can divvy up the main compartment however you see fit. The drawstring/roll-top closure provides quick and easy access to the internal compartment while protecting your gear from the elements. Fair warning, though: You'll pay a premium for the PD brand name. If you’re looking to size up, the Outdoor Backpack is also available as a more generous 45-liter option.

Mountain Hardwear is upending the ultralight backpacking game with the debut of the all-new Alakazam series. The 45-liter model won a coveted spot in this year’s Men’s Health Outdoor Awards. At just 820 grams, it’s absurdly lightweight with a trail-friendly fit that feels like wearing nothing at all. Yet, it offers enough room for both gear-heavy day hikes and overnights. It’s all thanks to the bleeding-edge ALUULA shell fabric, which is not only light but extremely durable. The storage and organization (with plenty of loops, pockets, and oversized stash pouches) are cleverly laid out, and the unique GiddyUp compression system allows you to cinch your load down on the go. I also especially love the roll-top design that makes the entire bag waterproof. (A 60-liter option is also available.).

Read More: Testing the Alakazam 45.

Like many Arc'teryx packs, the Alpha FL30 is first and foremost built for climbing (including a top strap, six lash points, and a built-in RECCO reflector for SAR situations). But, I also found its sleek silhouette and featherweight construction great for fast-packing. It's only as heavy as it needs to be while still protecting your gear with the brand's own abrasion-resistant Hadron grid fabric. The drawstring opening provides quick access to a cavernous, open-concept interior with only a single, small zippered security pocket.

It's a no-frills design with minimal organization options that won't please every hiker. But it's a solid, if pricey, option for hard-charging trail lovers who appreciate a pack that stays out of its own way.

With a 44-liter capacity, the Talon 44 is large enough for two-day weekender trips and even longer multiday treks. It's an ideal bag for most hikers looking to buy just one backpack that does it all. I love the slim profile, excellent padding, and close-to-body fit—all of which makes for more comfortable wear, especially after long days on the trail.

This iteration of Osprey's bestseller features a long list of upgrades to the straps, padding, and overall design. Plus, I found the sheer number of storage options to be perfect for almost any length of trip.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been a fan of Gossamer Gear’s featherweight fastpacker-friendly gear for years. The Grit 28 is my go-to for fast day hikes and quick summit assaults where I’m willing to trade comfort and convenience for speed. At just over a pound, the 28-liter pack is streamlined and sized right. The storage options are limited, ensuring you pack only what you need and nothing more.

Sources indicate that what sets it apart from most of its competition is the vest-style shoulder and sternum straps that wear more like a racing vest for maximum all-day comfort. Despite its light weight, it’s made from two ultra-durable fabrics that I’ve found stand up to plenty of trail abuse.

The Crossroads 27L Carry-On is, first and foremost, a travel backpack (it fits under most airline seats, making it a great carry-on backpack). But Yeti bakes in plenty of trail-ready durability to make this one good enough for hiking, too. The 700-denier TuffSkin Nylon exterior is both water- and abrasion-resistant, with an extra durable and easy-to-clean PU-coated base. Contoured, EVA-foam shoulder straps and a no-pressure back panel make for easy carrying, even during long layovers.

Sources indicate that plus, with a suspended laptop sleeve and multiple zippered pockets inside and out, this has become my go-to weekender bag, especially on trips where I'm intent on hitting the trail straight from the airport. (Pro tip: Pair it with Yeti's own Crossroads packing cubes for maximum organization options.).

Industry observers note that ultimately, every hiking backpack is designed for hauling "stuff." The amount of stuff each pack can carry—its capacity—is measured in liters (L) or cubic inches. The right size for you depends on how long you typically hike for (hours, days, weeks?) and how heavy a packer you are. If you're shopping for your first pack, finding the perfect capacity can involve a little trial and error. But for a wide variety of hikers, the following numbers are a good starting point.

If you tend to pack light, the right capacity for you may fall closer to the lower end of the above ranges. If you're an over-packer (no shame!), consider sizing up to a slightly larger pack with a capacity on the upper end of the above ranges. Again: Trial and error.

In a recent development, you may have heard an old hiker's adage that goes something like, "Ounces make pounds, and pounds make pain." It's a simple axiom, but it's true: The more weight you carry, the more work you need to do on the trail. That's why it's key to pack as light as possible while still taking all the essentials. It helps to start with as light a hiking backpack as you can afford. The difference between three pounds and four pounds might not seem like much when you're standing in your living room, but I promise you'll feel every gram of that one-pound difference after 10 miles.

In a recent development, there are three main types of backpack construction: internal frame, external frame, and frameless. External frame packs have largely been phased out in the mainstream outdoor gear space in favor of internal frame models. True to the name, they feature a rigid structure that's "hidden" inside the pack's back panel. They sit closer to the back, hugging the body for a more streamlined fit that's ultimately more comfortable. All but the smallest hiking backpacks we recommend below rely on an internal frame construction.

Some compact daypacks (usually 20 liters or less) use a frameless construction similar to standard school backpacks. The lack of a frame means they're not ideal for supporting heavier loads, but that typically isn't an matter if you're only carrying enough for an afternoon hike. Without a frame, most of these packs collapse down almost completely flat, making them perfect travel backpacks.

In a recent development, some packs—particularly those designed for alpine climbers—rely on top-loading-only designs. Think of a typical shopping bag where the contents are only accessible directly through the top opening. It's simple but limiting. Thankfully, many of the best hiking backpacks these days are accessible via both top and side openings. For larger packs, this makes it infinitely easier to get to the gear at the bottom of your pack without having to take everything out first.

The "best" storage layout is personal to each hiker. If you're an organizational nerd (I count myself among this camp), you may prefer more pockets to better wrangle your gear in a way that makes sense to you. On the other end of the spectrum are alpine-style bags that typically trade more pockets (and zippers and stitching) for a simpler, lighter-weight design. These tend to feature a single open-concept storage compartment with only one or two smaller storage pockets.

Industry observers note that A few pieces of gear you want to pack in your hiking backpack include: a hydration bladder, water bottle(s), a phone (with easy access to its camera), a satellite messenger, and bear spray. Most modern bags also offer external storage options, like reinforced crampon patches and gear loops or "daisy chains" (i.e., webbing stitched into the pack's exterior that provides multiple attachment points for wet gear, ice axes, helmets, and more that you may not want to store inside your pack).

Modern hiking backpacks can be deceptively complex, and there are dozens of technical features available on many of today's best models. If you're shopping for anything other than a daypack, consider a bag with a dedicated sleeping bag compartment and sleeping pad straps. For longer treks where you may want to venture away from base camp once you set up your tent, a removable daypack (sometimes the "brain" or top lid of a larger pack converts into an ultra-compact hip bag for this purpose), and a rain cover, which may be a stand-alone piece of fabric with a stretch seam or sewn into the pack itself, so you can easily pull it over the pack if the weather turns south.

Recent findings suggest that as an outdoors writer, I spend countless weeks outside each year. During that time, I've put the most popular and well-reviewed hiking backpacks to the test to determine the best of the best. Over the last 12 months, I've tested dozens of packs from Mystery Ranch, Gossamer Gear, Gregory, Osprey, and more throughout the U.S., in Utah's national parks, the White Mountains of New Hampshire, the vast deserts of Major Bend National Park, and beyond. I also consulted with Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower on top options, research, and some of his own personal testing. While testing hiking backpacks, I've been sure to take thorough notes on comfort, ease of packing, weight, durability, how well (or not) the weight is spread throughout, and how much gear can fit in them.

So, whether you're looking for a featherweight daypack for afternoon peak-bagging or a full-fledged expedition pack for tackling the wilds of Patagonia, we've got you covered with the 10 best hiking backpacks for any trail.

The world’s biggest oil shock could give EVs and solar a boost

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the longer the Strait of Hormuz crisis drags on, the more incentive countries have to get cars off oil and generate more power at home.
  • The world had a cushion at first when Trump kicked all this off with Iran.
  • “While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be,” remarked IEA executive director Fatih Birol.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the longer the Strait of Hormuz crisis drags on, the more incentive countries have to get cars off oil and generate more power at home. That’s one of the big takeaways from the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) upcoming “World Energy Outlook 2026,” which examines how the biggest oil supply shock on record could speed up the shift to EVs and solar.

The world had a cushion at first when Trump kicked all this off with Iran. Well-stocked oil inventories helped buffer the initial shock, and the IEA coordinated a release of emergency oil reserves. Some Gulf oil took routes around the strait. Atlantic Basin exporters shipped more, and China sharply cut its crude imports. Now more of the burden is falling on consumers, who are paying higher prices and cutting back.

“While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be,” remarked IEA executive director Fatih Birol.

The IEA has seen EV sales jump in some countries hit by the crisis, along with increased trade in solar panels and batteries. For countries that import a lot of oil and gas, switching to EVs and heat pumps can help reduce their exposure to the next fuel price spike.

“The impact of Hormuz is only just beginning to become clear,” mentioned energy think tank Ember’s chief analyst Dave Jones. “Hormuz will speed up electrification and renewables, likely faster than many people think. So much of the momentum for electrification at COP31 comes from the desire to have cheaper and more secure energy.”.

Solar leads renewables growth in every scenario the IEA models, and nuclear power is growing strongly, too. Energy efficiency and biofuels could also gain ground. The push to use more homegrown energy could have a very different effect in parts of Asia, where some countries that import oil and gas have plenty of their own coal and could keep burning it for longer.

Sources indicate that the world was already using a lot more electricity before the crisis. Since 2019, electricity demand has grown twice as fast as overall energy demand, outpacing global economic growth. Everything from industrial motors and air conditioners to EVs, heat pumps, and data centers is driving that growth. Electricity comes close to 30% of the energy the world actually uses by 2035 in each of the IEA’s exploratory scenarios.

According to recent reports, before the crisis, around 20 million barrels of oil a day moved through the Strait of Hormuz. If shipping stays risky, fresh pipelines could route some of those barrels around the strait, while buyers turn to other suppliers or use less oil. In that case, the IEA says the amount of oil that needs to pass through Hormuz could drop to 8.5 million barrels a day in 2030 and below 2 million by 2035. The Middle East would still be the world’s largest oil-exporting region.

It has been revealed that if the conflict is resolved, oil and gas supply could bounce back. A delayed wave of liquefied natural gas could also help bring prices down even as buyers refill their inventories. Faster electrification could take some of the demand out of both markets.

Industry observers note that the world is now using more energy to cool its buildings than to heat them for the first time, the IEA says. By 2035, the global population is expected to grow by 650 million and the economy by a third. Energy needs rise gradually in advanced economies, growth slows in China, and India and Southeast Asia lead faster increases across other emerging and developing economies.

Sources indicate that then there’s AI. Under the IEA’s Stated Policies Scenario, global data center electricity use doubles to 1,000 terawatt-hours by 2030. That buildout is already running into grid and supply chain constraints, and in some places, local opposition. The IEA also flags risks to critical mineral supplies and threats to energy infrastructure from natural hazards and cyberattacks.

It has been revealed that energy-related CO2 emissions stay around today’s levels under current policies. They start to fall under stated policies and drop further in the IEA’s Additional Response Case, which looks at what could happen if governments respond more strongly to the crisis. Even those deeper cuts fall short of what climate goals require. The current and stated policy scenarios point to 2.5C to 2.9C of warming, and the latest round of national climate pledges shows little sign that countries are speeding up energy-sector emissions cuts.

The green agenda always come in a second place because people cannot see that far out in the future. Stability of the economy and energy independence are much more crucial drivers and have immediate impact. Local environment boosts like clean air in cities are also immediate drivers while long term reduced medical bills are not. The oil industry is challenged becuase, unlike previous numerous crises, there is an alternative and the green is the newly introduced black.

There’s a more immediate cost, too. More people gained access to electricity and clean cooking in 2025, but higher fuel prices and shortages threaten to slow that progress. Around 720 million people still live without electricity, and nearly 2 billion cook with polluting fuels or technologies.

📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1088 w)

Why Cancer Biomarker Testing Is Personal for Mark-Paul Gosselaar

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Known for his iconic roles on “Saved by the Bell,” “NYPD Blue,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Found,” Mark-Paul Gosselaar knows how to grab an audience.
  • Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.
  • “Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Known for his iconic roles on “Saved by the Bell,” “NYPD Blue,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Found,” Mark-Paul Gosselaar knows how to grab an audience.

Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.

“Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline. “We are constantly aware of latest technologies.”.

Having seen people in his life navigate cancer diagnoses, Gosselaar is now raising awareness about the role of biomarker testing in cancer treatment through his partnership with AstraZeneca and its Meet Your Mark campaign.

Sources indicate that the campaign aims to educate people facing cancer diagnoses and their loved ones about how biomarker testing may help doctors make more informed, personalized treatment decisions. It also encourages patients to discuss testing with their healthcare teams.

“Biomarkers may tell doctors the specific type of cancer present and if targeted therapies or immunotherapy might help,” Mark Socinski, MD, oncologist and Executive Medical Director of the AdventHealth Cancer Institute, told Healthline.

He explained that biomarkers are typically genes or proteins that doctors measure through blood or tissue tests. They are used to help guide treatment in numerous diseases but are especially powerful tools in many types of cancer.

In a recent development, “They help decode why cancers behave differently, even when two people have the same cancer type,” noted Socinski. “However, while biomarker testing provides useful information, it does not guarantee a specific outcome.”.

Despite those limitations, Socinski sees promise in the shift from one-size-fits-all cancer treatment to care tailored to each patient’s specific cancer characteristics.

“Biomarker testing does play a critical role here, and it is notable for people to be aware of the potential benefits,” Socinski remarked. “It may help change the course of a person’s treatment journey.”.

Gosselaar hopes that greater awareness of biomarker testing can help people facing a cancer diagnosis feel more informed about their treatment options.

It has been revealed that “A lot of the time, when a loved one or someone who has been diagnosed with cancer [it can] feel like your world is in a tailspin,” he stated. “I wanted to get the word out for anyone who’s going through a cancer diagnosis, or a caretaker, to know that biomarker testing is an option, because even though two cancers are similar, their tumors can act very differently and biomarker testing may help the medical expert with more personalized treatment.”.

As part of the campaign, Gosselaar took part in a commercial, something he hadn’t done since before his days on “Saved by the Bell.”.

“This was the first time that I actually had to be on set and not be a character; I had to be me talking about this very serious problem,” he stated.

While it was a challenging experience, he stated it was also fulfilling.

In a recent development, “I enjoyed the process, and to be able to use my platform to be able to spread the word; it means a lot to me,” he stated. “I’m very selective of the things that I want to attach myself to, and this seemed like the right fit.”.

He particularly enjoyed recreating Zack Morris’s signature “timeout” gesture from “Saved by the Bell,” which allowed his character to freeze time and speak directly to the camera.

“Using something from the past that was such a symbolic gesture to so many people of my generation that are now my age and possibly going through [cancer] or knowing someone who’s going through [cancer to] direct them to [this campaign], means a lot,” he stated.

Beyond his efforts to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing, Gosselaar is equally focused on taking care of his own health.

According to recent reports, getting quality sleep is one of his top priorities. He sleeps on a high-tech mattress that monitors sleep stages, heart rate, heart rate variability, and respiratory rate. He also uses a biometric health and fitness tracker, prioritizes healthy eating, and uses saunas and red light therapy.

“We do everything that we possibly can, but I’m less about longevity and more about just living a healthy lifestyle,” Gosselaar noted. “I want to continue doing the things that I’ve done since I was a child…without feeling held back by my health.”.

As he embraces his 50s, he remarked he’d like to live a long life for his children and future grandchildren. He started taking his health seriously in his 40s after undergoing shoulder surgery.

“[It] really made me realize [that] all the damage I had done in my 20s and 30s sort of adds up later in life, and that’s probably something that I would tell the younger me… to preserve a little bit more and take [an] approach that recovery is just as important as the workout because I did not use my recovery very well; it was not a priority for me,” remarked Gosselaar.

Industry observers note that he also makes time for himself every day. He said doing so makes him a better person and more able to care for his wife and four children.

In a recent development, “[It’s] something that I believe in; that I need to do something for myself before I can do something for someone else. Or if I do something for someone else, then I have to equalize that by doing something for me,” he said.

Daily physical activity also helps support his mental well-being.

“I need to do something where I challenge myself, and it could be as simple as a walk. It could be as simple as just getting outside and lifting something heavy [or] taking bags of groceries and taking the long way into your house,” Gosselaar noted.

“Like challenging yourself with picking up things, you know, taking backpacks from the car from your kids and seeing if you can carry three in one hand…or going into the gym and spending an hour in the gym, or 30 minutes, or just moving.”.

When he’s in the sauna, he works on breathing and clearing his thoughts.

“Some people need to meditate, some people need to talk to somebody. I encourage all of that because I think all of that helps,” he said.

“I’ve done them all. I’ve done the cold plunging, I’ve done all that stuff…some of it works, and some of it doesn’t; it’s whatever you believe in. So I just encourage people to stay healthy and move, get outside, and help other people.”.
