#109758. I ride e-bikes for a living. This is the real gear I actually use

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3764 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

I ride e-bikes for a living. This is the real gear I actually use

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3764 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m in the somewhat unusual position of basically riding electric bicycles for a living.
  • Sources indicate that of course I don’t just ride e-bikes for work.
  • Sources indicate that in other words: I talk the talk and I walk the walk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m in the somewhat unusual position of basically riding electric bicycles for a living. I’ve been working with e-bikes for nearly two decades, professionally covering the e-bike industry for most of that time, testing hundreds of different models and traveling around the world to ride newly introduced e-bikes in some pretty incredible places. Yeah, it’s a tough job – but someone’s got to suffer it.

Sources indicate that of course I don’t just ride e-bikes for work. I ride them recreationally. I ride them for exercise. I ride them for transportation. My family doesn’t even own a car, meaning two wheels handle the vast majority of our transportation.

Sources indicate that in other words: I talk the talk and I walk the walk. Or perhaps more accurately, I ride the ride.

And while most of the time all you really need for a good ride is an e-bike and a direction to go in, there are a handful of pieces of gear that I’ve come to rely on over the years. Some keep me safer. Some keep my bikes out of the hands of thieves. Some make rides more comfortable or convenient. And some are just neat little things that I’ve discovered along the way.

This isn’t a list of every bike accessory I’ve ever tested, nor am I saying these are necessarily the absolute best products in every category. These are simply the things that I actually use. Some are a bit pricey, some are dirt cheap (several pieces of gear below are under $5!), but they’re all things I personally rely on and that I recommend to my friends and family. And now, to you.

If you own nice e-bikes, you’re eventually going to spend a lot of time thinking about locks. Your lock may even be your most vital accessory. Or perhaps I should say “accessories”, because the best way to ensure your e-bike is still there when you get back is to use more than one solid lock.

My go-to options that I grab basically every day for the last couple of years have been Seatylock’s FoldyLock Forever folding lock and Mason 220 U-lock.

For reference, the Foldylock Forever is the world’s strongest folding lock. That’s not just their marketing speak, but rather it’s confirmed by independent testing and certification. It’s the only folding lock in the world to achieve an ART 3-star security rating awarded by the Stichting ART Foundation, an independent Dutch organization that tests and certifies anti-theft locks. It earned that certification three years ago, and no other folding lock has been able to reach that level yet. The only higher ratings ART gives are for locks rated for motorcycles.

Personally, I like folding locks because they pack relatively neatly on the bike while still giving me enough flexibility to work around different racks and poles, or even larger things like trees.

The FoldyLock Forever is the one I reach for when I want serious security matched with more flexibility, while the Mason 220 gives me another beefy option when I know a U-lock will fit what I’m locking to.

In a recent development, the Mason is great as a strong U-lock, but I also like how large it is, letting me lock to wider poles and also a tad bit farther from the pole itself, leaving room for pannier bags and other things that get in the way. Amazingly, it’s also one of the few U-locks I have that can fit over the beefy battery-filled downtube on most of my e-bikes.

I also use the smaller FoldyLock Compact when I want something easier to carry and don’t need quite as much lock.

It’s more affordable and lighter, though it doesn’t have quite the same security level as the bigger and beefier options above.

Sources indicate that the Compact does have one other advantage, though: it comes in all sorts of bright colors and even a rainbow option where each link is a different color. That might not be a huge security concern, but it’s fun when you can choose a color to match your bike or mood!

No bike lock makes a bicycle theft-proof. Given enough time and the right tools, a determined thief can defeat virtually anything. The idea is to make your bike enough of a pain in the butt to steal that the thief decides someone else’s bike looks easier. And if they still want your bike (because let’s face it, you’ve probably got an awesome e-bike), then the multiple locks better be good ones so its takes them long enough that they eventually give up.

Recent findings suggest that I also covered Seatylock’s upcoming angle grinder-proof U-locks that I saw at the Milan Motorcycle Show, so I’ll likely switch to those once they come out this Spring. They’re designed to keep motorcycles safe, and come in two sizes: one for motorcycles and a smaller one for bikes.

Let’s continue with what may actually be the most important piece of gear for an e-biker: a helmet.

I’ve tested plenty of helmets over the years, but lately I’ve been gravitating toward UNIT 1’s helmets. They’re comfortable, they look good, and I appreciate the extra safety features beyond simply putting a layer of impact protection around my skull.

It has been revealed that I particularly like having integrated lighting built right into my helmet, putting lights up high where they’re easier for drivers to see. On models like the FARO, I also appreciate the inclusion of MIPS as well as the handlebar-mounted remote for activating the helmet’s turn signals.

According to recent reports, I recently started using UNIT 1’s NEON helmet too, which is lighter and has a really slick magnetic face shield. You barely have to line the shield up; get it close enough and the magnets practically snatch it out of your hand and put it into place. It’s clear enough for night riding but darkens in bright sunlight, and the helmet is rated for faster 28 mph e-bike riding.

There are cheaper helmets out there, of course, but considering how much time I spend on two wheels, a good helmet is one area where I don’t mind spending a bit more.

You can actually see the FARO helmet in the clip below, along with the TriEye glasses coming up next.

In a recent development, triEye glasses are another accessory that sounds a little gimmicky until you actually start using them. Sunglasses with a built-in rearview mirror? I was sure they were going to be a gimmick but they just looked too interesting to pass up, so I offered to test them out.

As it turns out, they’re now the first sunglasses I reach for when I’m riding. They really do work!

They have a tiny rear-view mirror integrated into the glasses, giving me a quick view behind me without having to turn my head all the way around.

It takes a little time to get used to looking into such a small mirror, but once your brain figures it out, it becomes surprisingly natural. I can rapidly check what’s approaching from behind while still keeping most of my attention pointed forward.

It’s especially useful when riding on roads where I’m regularly interacting with traffic, though I still give an old-fashioned head check before making any major lateral move.

They’re $99, which isn’t bad for decent sunglasses, though you can get them for 10% off with the discount code EBIKE at checkout.

I love listening to music and podcasts while riding, but I’m not a fan of plugging my ears while sharing the road with cars.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why I’ve become a big fan of H2O Audio’s bone-conduction headphones. They sit outside my ears and transmit sound through bone conduction, meaning my ears themselves remain open to the world around me. I’ve been testing out the latest TRI ULTRA PRO model, and it’s pretty dang amazing! I can hear my music perfectly, but I can still hear all the road sounds, pedestrians, other cyclists, etc.

Of course, that doesn’t mean you can crank the music and magically retain perfect situational awareness. But at reasonable volumes, I can enjoy something in the background while still hearing cars, horns, bells and everything else happening around me.

For longer recreational rides especially, they’ve become one of those things I really appreciate having along. I’ve done rides as long as 3 hours with them and they haven’t felt cumbersome or made my ears sore, so the fit seems great for me.

Sources indicate that I really like the Knog Oi Prima as a bike bell. It looks good, has a nice low-profile design and does what a bell is supposed to do without looking like you bolted a miniature doorbell onto your handlebars.

In a recent development, despite its small size, it’s also super loud. And unlike the older ratcheting-style bells (krr-krr-krr-krrring), this is a single thumper, meaning I can ding once promptly for a polite “hello, I’m here!” or several hard and rapid DINGs for a “wtf do you think you’re doing, guy?!”.

In a recent development, the bell absolutely disappears on my handlebars, which is good because there’s not much real estate left up there. Really, the only downside I can find is that it’s not cheap, at around $32 depending on current sales.

But I also have another favorite bell that costs a fraction as much.

According to recent reports, I found cheap bike bells on AliExpress that have a hidden compartment for an Apple AirTag. From the outside, it just looks like a boring bike bell. Inside, it’s secretly helping me keep tabs on my bike.

And for $4, they’re a pretty awesome deal for a loud bell that hides a tracking device. Of course, you’ll have to fork over another $20 or so for the AirTag tracker, but your e-bike is certainly worth that much.

Which brings me to another part of my bike security strategy.

It has been revealed that I don’t necessarily stop at one AirTag. One AirTag is for amateurs. I go with multiple. A four-pack is $79, or around half the cost of a solid e-bike lock.

There are all sorts of clever AirTag hiding accessories available now. In addition to the bell, I’ve used a $5 water bottle-style AirTag holder as well as an $8 rear reflector with a hidden AirTag compartment.

According to recent reports, the reflector isn’t the most inconspicuous AirTag hider, but the water bottle holder definitely doesn’t scream “guess what’s actually inside of my molded plastic body!” And for added security, the water bottle holder is held on with Torx bolts. It’s not exactly a security key, but even if a bike thief carries hex wrenches with them, they’re unlikely to have Torx wrenches, meaning that the AirTag will stay on the bike a bit longer while it’s in the hands of a thief.

It has been revealed that airTags aren’t dedicated anti-theft GPS trackers, and Apple intentionally includes anti-stalking features that can eventually alert someone that an unknown AirTag is traveling with them. But I still think they’re a useful additional layer of security, especially because they’re cheap enough to use redundantly.

Industry observers note that A bike thief might know enough to search for an AirTag and remove it. But are they going to keep searching after they find the first one? What about the second? Are they expecting three?

According to recent reports, that’s the idea, anyway. And since I keep pretty good tabs on my e-bikes, I’ll know pretty rapidly if one goes missing. From there, it’s a race between me getting to the thief and him finding all of my AirTags. Good luck, buddy.

I’m a big believer in wearing proper protective gear when riding faster electric two-wheelers, but I also don’t particularly want to look like I’m headed to a motorcycle race every time I leave the house. That’s one of the reasons I’ve really come to appreciate my Beyond Riders protective riding hoodie.

According to recent reports, it looks and feels much like a regular casual hoodie, but it’s designed with motorcycle-style protection in mind, including abrasion-resistant materials and removable impact protectors. Believe it or not, there’s flexible CE Level 2 armor in there on the elbows, shoulders, chest, and spine.

Industry observers note that I like that I can throw it on before a ride and get an extra layer of protection without having to wear a bulky motorcycle jacket. It’s particularly nice for faster e-bikes and electric mopeds, where the speeds are high enough that I’d rather have something more substantial than a regular sweatshirt between my skin and the pavement.

Industry observers note that of course, no protective hoodie is going to make a crash harmless, and I still choose my gear based on the type of riding I’m doing. But I love products that make it easier to incorporate safety into everyday riding without adding a bunch of hassle. If protective gear is comfortable, convenient, and looks good enough that I actually want to wear it, that’s a big win in my book.

In a recent development, tannus tire liners are perhaps one of the less exciting products on this list, right up until they save you from fixing a flat on the side of the road. And then they’re the one thing on this list you’ll be ready to open-mouth kiss.

I’ve used Tannus products for years as an extra layer of flat protection, and I’m a massive believer in them.

No tire protection system is going to prevent every possible flat, but anything that reduces my chances of sitting on the side of a road pulling a wheel off an e-bike is worth considering.

That’s particularly true with e-bikes, where hub motor wheels can be more complicated to remove thanks to heavy motors, annoying cables, clumsy torque washers, and other hardware.

According to recent reports, tannus tire liners are annoying to install, but you do it once and forget about it. Then you’re almost guaranteed to not get a flat.

And even if you do happen to get a 3″ nail going through it at the perfect angle, they serve as runflats so you can still ride home (albeit a bit slower and more carefully) instead of doing the walk of shame next to your bike.

I don’t want to carry an entire bike shop with me, but I do want enough tools to deal with the common things that can happen during a ride.

According to recent reports, the Topeak Ratchet Stick hits a nice sweet spot for me. It’s small enough that I’ll actually bring it along, yet useful enough for the various bolts and adjustments that tend to crop up on bikes.

All of the crucial bits fit right inside the handle, so I don’t have any extra sleeves or clips to keep tabs on.

This is exactly what I want from a ride tool: something small but effective. The giant tool kit sitting at home isn’t particularly useful when something starts rattling 20 kilometers away.

At $48, it’s not cheap. But I’ve had mine for around 6 years, and it’s still going strong, so at least it’s well made! At around 8 bucks per year, I’d call it a good investment.

This is one of my more recent cheap finds.

I picked up a waterproof-style pannier bag from AliExpress for around $25, and I’ve been surprisingly impressed with it.

It isn’t quite as big as the pannier I have from Priority Bicycles, but it still holds a useful amount of cargo and feels much nicer than I expected for the price.

I particularly like that there are two ways to close it. You can use it as a traditional roll-top pannier and clip the sides together, or you can use the strap that comes over the top when you have too much stuff in there to close it the normal way. I use that second option anytime I have my yoga mat in there since it sticks out the top, but I can still close it relatively tight to keep the mat from swinging around while riding. Depending on how much stuff I’m carrying and how I’ve packed it, having both options is quite convenient.

It has been revealed that it’s not the fanciest pannier I own. But for around 25 bucks, it’s one of those cheap accessories that turned out to be much better than I expected.

These might have the highest usefulness-to-price ratio of anything here.

I bought a pair of tiny plastic handlebar jacks on AliExpress for barely more than a dollar. They clip onto the handlebars and provide little stands for when I need to turn a bicycle upside down.

Anyone who has ever flipped a modern e-bike over to change a tube knows the problem. Your handlebars are probably covered in displays, buttons, brake levers, bells, phone mounts and who knows what else. Turning the bike upside down means resting all of that expensive stuff directly on the ground.

You can loosen everything and rotate it out of the way. Or you can use two $1 pieces of plastic.

According to recent reports, the jacks hold the handlebars slightly above the ground so my accessories don’t get scratched or crushed. Simple problem, simple solution.

If you have a 3D printer, you can probably just print your own version of these. There’s a rubber O-ring-style keeper on it, but you can probably just use a rubber band if you wanted to DIY these yourself.

Another recent addition has been a ZOOM suspension dropper seatpost that I installed on my Ride1Up Roadster V3.

It has been revealed that I love the thing now that it’s installed. It gives me suspension to take some of the sting out of rough roads while also providing the convenience of a dropper post.

Getting it onto my particular bike, however, was another story.

Sources indicate that it took me nearly two hours, largely because the Ride1Up Roadster V3 wasn’t set up for the internal cable routing I needed. I got the cable most of the way there through the downtube’s very narrow wire run, but then I ultimately ended up drilling a small hole in the seat tube to make the last bit of my installation work.

To be very clear: I do not recommend doing that.

Sources indicate that drilling holes in bicycle frames can compromise their structural integrity, void warranties and generally create problems you don’t want. As a mechanical engineer with a lot of bike experience, I was comfortable making that decision on my own bike because I knew exactly where the frame is least stressed, but it’s definitely not something I’d advise others to copy.

Recent findings suggest that the lesson here isn’t “drill your frame.” It’s to check whether your bike is actually designed for an internally routed dropper post before ordering one. Had I done that first (basically by shining a flashlight down the empty seat tube and realizing there wasn’t a hole to access the bottom bracket), I could have saved myself quite a bit of trouble and just gotten a dropper post with an external cable run.

But now that it’s installed? I love it!

And finally, here’s one that isn’t really normal bike gear at all, but that I LOVE bringing on my rides.

I spend a lot of time taking photos and videos of bikes, which presents an obvious problem when I’m both the cyclist and the photographer.

The HOVERAir X1 Pro Max has become one of my favorite solutions. It’s a tiny autonomous flying camera that can follow me around without requiring someone else to pilot it. I used the previous version of this drone for a while until this version came out, and then I immediately upgraded.

It folds down small enough that I basically forget that I even have it in my bag. Despite its small size, it still can automatically track and follow me, even at speeds of over 20 mph (32 km/h). That means I can pull it out during a ride, send it up (it takes off from my palm!) and get tracking shots that would normally require another person riding or running alongside me with a camera.

I especially like the Dolly Track mode, which can create some fantastic moving shots while automatically following me from the sides or the front, instead of just the boring old follow-behind-me drone shots you usually see.

Industry observers note that just be aware that its obstacle avoidance isn’t great when flying sideways or backward, meaning I’ve flown it into walls, fences, and street signs plenty of times already. But I can also report back that somehow the little guy is still working fine. I’m not suggesting that’s part of the official durability testing procedure, but it has certainly become part of mine. Now it’s my go-to drone, and I especially like bringing it on my travels for all the same reasons.

After a list this long, I should probably point out that you don’t actually need most of this stuff.

According to recent reports, that’s one of the things I love about bikes. You don’t need a pile of expensive gear to have a good time. Most days, give me an e-bike, a helmet and a direction to point the front wheel, and I’m happy.

But after years of riding e-bikes professionally, recreationally, for exercise and simply to get around, these are the products that I’ve found myself continuing to use.

Industry observers note that sure, some of these are expensive pay-to-play things that are a lot of fun but might not be worth it for the casual rider. And some are just $1 pieces of plastic that keep me from smashing my bike computer into the pavement.

But they’ve all found their way into my life after being battle-tested… and passing!

#109756. Tech Report: What Children Really Notice About Honesty

Tech Report: What Children Really Notice About Honesty

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • In a recent development, as parents, most of us want to raise honest children.
  • Recent findings suggest that but there is another way children learn about honesty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

In a recent development, as parents, most of us want to raise honest children. We tell them honesty is important. We remind them to tell the truth when they make mistakes or do something wrong. We praise their honesty when they admit wrongdoing. And we explain why lying can damage trust.

Recent findings suggest that but there is another way children learn about honesty. They are not only listening to what we say. They are also watching what we do.

And sometimes those two things do not match.

According to recent reports, perhaps we tell our child that honesty is important but then claim they are younger than they really are to get a discounted movie ticket. Or we remind our child to take responsibility when they make mistakes, yet avoid taking responsibility for our own. Most of us can think of situations where our actions do not perfectly align with the messages we are trying to teach.

What do children make of these mixed messages?

According to recent reports, my colleagues and I recently conducted a study to explore this question. We wanted to understand how children think about honesty when parents' actions either support or contradict the lessons they teach.

It has been revealed that we recruited 127 children between 5 and 12 years of age. The children listened to stories about parents and their children. In some stories, the parent stressed the importance of honesty and then behaved honestly. In others, the parent promoted honesty but later engaged in dishonest behaviour. After each story, the children were asked what they thought about the parent and what lessons another child might learn from observing that parent.

One finding stood out: children noticed when parents' words and actions did not match. Parents who practised what they preached were viewed more positively than parents whose behaviour contradicted their message.

Even more interesting, when children's predictions depended on choosing between a parent's words and a parent's actions, they often gave greater weight to the parent's behaviour. In other words, when there was a conflict between what a parent stated and what a parent did, children frequently treated the behaviour as the more crucial source of information.

Children also viewed truthful parents as more trustworthy than parents who lied. Whether the lie was told to avoid hurting someone's feelings or to avoid getting into trouble mattered less than one might expect. The simple fact that the parent chose honesty influenced children's judgments. In short, children preferred parents whose actions matched the values they claimed to hold.

Sources indicate that our findings suggest that children are not simply listening to what parent say, they are also paying attention to what parents do. When parents’ actions are consistent with their messages about honesty, children receive a clear message about the value of truthfulness. When words and actions conflict, that message becomes more ambiguous.

According to recent reports, this does not mean parents must be perfect. Perfection is neither realistic nor necessary. However, parents should remember that everyday behaviour teaches powerful lessons. Children learn about honesty not only from conversations, but also from watching how adults handle mistakes, promises, responsibilities, and everyday challenges.

The findings suggest several practical ways parents can promote honesty.

In a recent development, parents often believe that the key to teaching honesty is telling children that honesty matters. That message is certainly important. But our research suggests that children are paying just as much attention to something else: whether we live by the values we teach.

When it comes to honesty, children appear to be asking not only, "What did my parent say?" but also, "What did my parent do?".

Bélanger, E., Crossman, A. M., & Talwar, V. (2026). Practice what you preach? Children’s evaluations of parents’ verbal messages and social modeling of honesty and lie-telling. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 268, 106528. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022096526000809.

Yosemite needs your help tracking river otters

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that el Capitan.
  • Even for experienced rangers and biologists, North American river otters (Lontra canadensis) are difficult to monitor.
  • Sources indicate that additionally, one otter can travel five to 10 miles a day along rivers and streams, making them difficult to track.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that el Capitan. Glowing waterfalls. Half dome. River otters. Yosemite National Park is home to all of these natural wonders and more. The plucky and playful mammals have officially been spotted in the population park in Northern California—and park rangers want the public’s help to monitor them.

Even for experienced rangers and biologists, North American river otters (Lontra canadensis) are difficult to monitor. They have a very high metabolism, and can eat about 15 to 20 percent of their body weight in a single day. They spend a lot of their time looking for prey, including fish, crayfish, crabs, frogs, birds’ eggs, and even some reptiles like turtles.

Sources indicate that additionally, one otter can travel five to 10 miles a day along rivers and streams, making them difficult to track. According to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, river otters’ range stretches all of Northern California’s five coastal counties from Oregon down to San Francisco Bay, the Sierra Nevada Mountains from Mariposa County north, and large parts of the inland northern valley. Yosemite National Park itself has over 1,700 miles of streams, so that’s a lot of wet ground to cover when looking for otters.

Park rangers are asking the public to note the location, date, and time of any river otter sightings in Yosemite. Written sightings can be reported in the comments section of this Facebook post or the park’s contact us form. Any videos or photos can be shared through a direct message on Instagram.

“Your observations can help us better understand how otters roam and use Yosemite’s waterways,” the rangers write.

River otters are not endangered, but they have had a rocky history. During the 19th and 20th centuries, they were extensively hunted and trapped for their fur and many were removed from their natural range. Decades of conservation and reintroduction efforts are at the moment helping populations to recover. California’s population is considered fairly stable, but they are still at risk from further habitat destruction and water pollution.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done. Having just released a upcoming patch - which already included several updates to Challenges and Assignments - Battlefield Studios has gone in and made even more changes.

This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.

The updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge. Now, any headshot beyond 75m will count. Recon Expert 3 is another headshot-themed one that’s been updated, and now requires getting headshot kills beyond 125m, rather than the practically impossible beyond 200m that it required previously.

According to recent reports, the Rapid Fire 2 Challenge, which required getting kills beyond 50m with Assault Rifles, has been changed so it now tracks anything beyond 40m. The painful ‘Inflict damage under 15m while hip-firing with Assault Rifles’ has been entirely replaced with one that requires - the far more sensible - inflicting damage while in ADS with Assault Rifles.

A couple of Challenges, such as the one that required suppressing enemies with LMGs, and another that wanted you to deal damage to laser-designated vehicles using lock-on weapons, have both been removed.

Recent findings suggest that the journey to make Challenges and Assignments easier to complete has been a long one. Progression has been one of the key areas of criticism Battlefield 6 received at launch. The glitch encompassed more than just slow player and weapon XP earn rates, it also prevented players from accessing latest Training Paths for the various classes, and several of the game's weapons.

Battlefield Studios attacked the problem from multiple angles, initially boosting the XP players and their weapons would earn, before later reducing the requirements of the Challenges themselves. The developer continued to streamline those requirements over multiple patches, including majorly overhauling the system earlier this month.

It seems the studio is more confident than ever in the game, as it recently announced that Battlefield 6 will be getting its first free trial next week, offering players who do not own the full game access to iconic modes like Conquest, and Breakthrough - though on an unusual selection of maps.

Industry News: 1 in 3 Infants Diagnosed With Peanut Allergy May Not Have the Condition

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Peanut allergies have been on the rise in recent decades.
  • According to statistics provided by Food Allergy Research & Education (FARE), an estimated 6.2 million children and adults in the United States are allergic to peanuts.
  • However, fresh research published in the November 2026 issue of The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology suggests that over a third of infants thought to have this diagnosis might not actually have a peanut allergy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Peanut allergies have been on the rise in recent decades.

According to statistics provided by Food Allergy Research & Education (FARE), an estimated 6.2 million children and adults in the United States are allergic to peanuts.

However, fresh research published in the November 2026 issue of The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology suggests that over a third of infants thought to have this diagnosis might not actually have a peanut allergy.

In fact, having a history of reacting to peanuts and positive allergy testing on their own may not be sufficient to diagnose a peanut allergy for many infants.

The study’s authors suggest that a threshold oral food challenge — in which the child is given increasing amounts of the suspected food allergen under medical supervision to look for an allergic reaction — should be routinely considered to help confirm peanut allergy.

This additional testing could safely prevent children who are not allergic to peanuts from undergoing unnecessary treatment with oral immunotherapy.

It could also spare families from burdensome food restrictions and allergy precautions.

The researchers’ goal was to evaluate the accuracy and safety of the Allergy Development to an Accelerated Path to Tolerance (ADAPT) peanut oral immunotherapy program, which was established in 2024 at 10 public children’s hospitals across Australia.

This program provides a standardized approach to evaluating and treating infants with suspected peanut allergies.

The study included infants who had experienced a mild to moderate reaction to peanut before 12 months of age and had evidence of peanut sensitization through allergy testing.

Researchers reviewed medical records to examine how accurately the program’s approach identified peanut allergies and whether it could safely guide treatment.

A key part of the evaluation was a threshold oral food challenge. The challenge involved up to seven doses, ranging from 15 to 1,300 milligrams of peanut protein.

Medical teams monitored the infants for reactions and provided treatment when necessary.

Researchers reviewed records from April 2024 through October 2025. During that period, 1,275 infants were assessed through the program, and 778 underwent an oral food challenge.

The researchers also examined allergy test results and whether infants who reacted during the challenges could begin oral immunotherapy at an appropriate starting dose.

At the time of the oral food challenge, the infants had a median age of 13 months.

Of the 778 infants who underwent an oral food challenge, 507 (65.2%) had an allergic reaction.

However, 271 (34.8%) did not react to peanut during the supervised test, despite having a history of a previous reaction and positive allergy test results.

These findings suggest that relying on medical history and allergy tests alone may lead some infants to be labeled with a peanut allergy when they can actually tolerate the food.

In a recent development, among the infants who reacted during the challenges, 61 experienced anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction that can affect breathing and blood pressure. This represented 12% of infants with a positive challenge and 7.8% of all infants who underwent testing. Medical teams safely managed these severe allergic reactions.

Researchers also found that infants who reacted to peanut generally had higher skin prick test results and Ara h 2-specific IgE levels than those who did not react.

However, these test results did not reliably indicate how much peanut would trigger a reaction or how severe that reaction would be.

Of the 394 infants who began peanut oral immunotherapy, 384 (97.5%) successfully started treatment at a dose below the amount that had triggered a reaction during their food challenge.

The researchers say these findings support considering supervised oral food challenges to confirm suspected peanut allergies before starting treatment or recommending long-term avoidance.

Erin Banta, MD, a board certified allergist and immunologist who treats both children and adults at Latitude Food Allergy Care in Great Neck, New York, said these findings are significant because they provide evidence for early use of oral food challenges in infants with peanut reactions.

“In those with mild-moderate prior reactions to peanut, early oral food challenge may allow for either delabeling of food allergy (in 1/3 of the patients in this study) or diagnosis of food allergy,” she told Healthline.

Banta, who wasn’t involved in the study, added that early delabeling takes a significant burden off the patient and their family.

“On the other hand,” she explained, “early diagnosis allows for early initiation of treatment with oral immunotherapy at a time in the patient’s life associated with the greatest success rates.”.

According to recent reports, banta further noted that the study offers different pathways for oral immunotherapy based on the patient’s reaction threshold. This means that some patients may be able to complete treatment more quickly due to their individual threshold dose.

Lindsey Forstie, FNP, a family nurse practitioner with clinical training and experience in allergy and asthma care at Carefree Allergy in Phoenix, AZ, added that while further evaluation may be needed to confirm a peanut allergy diagnosis, it’s key for parents not to try introducing peanuts at home.

“Instead, they should speak with their pediatrician or allergist about appropriate testing and whether a supervised food challenge is safe and necessary,” she remarked.

According to Forstie, who was also not part of the study, the goal is to avoid unnecessary food restrictions while also keeping children safe.

Recent findings suggest that “The key message is that not every positive allergy test means a child has a food allergy,” she told Healthline. “Accurate diagnosis helps protect children while allowing those who are not allergic to enjoy a more normal, less restrictive diet.”.

Our 5th Time Hosting the Hudson Quattrocento Rally Was Unforgettable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that road & Track just returned from our fifth Hudson Quattrocento rally, and this year’s festivities were a familiar reminder of why we can’t stay away from Upstate New York.
  • Drivers indicated out with a diverse lineup of cars: a 2026 Bentley Continental GTC Speed, a 2000 Ferrari 456M GT, a 2026 Lotus Emira, and even a Cinnabar Red 1988 BMW M6.
  • It has been revealed that day one of Hudson Quattrocento kicked off at Scribner’s Catskill Lodge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that road & Track just returned from our fifth Hudson Quattrocento rally, and this year’s festivities were a familiar reminder of why we can’t stay away from Upstate New York. A special group of readers from across the United States and Canada spent four days driving through the Hudson Valley and Catskill Mountains, touring the greatest roads from past rallies and exploring some all-new pavement, too. Fun fact: the “quattrocento” in the rally’s namesake comes from the Italian word for “four hundred”, alluding to the four-hundred-mile route of our first-ever Hudson Quattrocento rally. This year, we gave participants an extra 80 miles, plus a couple of surprises along the way.

Drivers indicated out with a diverse lineup of cars: a 2026 Bentley Continental GTC Speed, a 2000 Ferrari 456M GT, a 2026 Lotus Emira, and even a Cinnabar Red 1988 BMW M6. The drive was led by Editor-in-Chief Dan Pund in an Aston Martin Vanquish Volante, Editor-at-Large Matt Farah in a Ford Mustang Dark Horse SC, and Executive Editor Mike Austin in a Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing. Our official event partner, Corient, also came along for the ride to help make Hudson Quattrocento an unforgettable rally.

It has been revealed that day one of Hudson Quattrocento kicked off at Scribner’s Catskill Lodge. Guests checked in at registration, grabbed a light bite, got briefed on the rally’s road rules, and listened to introductions from Road & Track staff and fellow attendees.

In a recent development, rally participants lined up in their driving groups for the first route—an out-and-back joyride to Rhinebeck, NY. Peak autumn offers a magical driving experience in the Hudson Valley, with winding roads lined with bursts of red, orange, and yellow leaves and the crisp sting of not-yet-cold fall air.

According to recent reports, in Rhinebeck, we stopped for lunch at Gigi Trattoria and afforded guests time to explore the charming Hudson Valley town. We hopped back in our cars and completed the loop back to Scribner’s Catskill Lodge, where guests checked into their rooms and explored the woodsy property.

According to recent reports, after a little downtime, we gathered for drinks and dinner in the Apex Lounge. Later, we took full advantage of being in the chilly mountains by gathering around a cozy firepit and enjoying s’mores. Guests then tucked in for the night and rested up for the following day’s track activities.

In a recent development, guests started Day Two with breakfast at the hotel before lining up in our driving groups. The group headed west to Wilzig Racing Manor, a private, Grand Prix-style racing circuit in entrepreneur and semi-pro driver Alan Wilzig’s backyard. This exclusive track is not typically open to the public, so getting a turn at the 1.1-mile road course was a real privilege. After lapping the elevation-heavy road course, we also got the chance to explore Wilzig’s unreal collection of classic cars, race cars, and motorcycles. From the 2006 Ariel Atom and 2008 Lotus 2-Eleven to the 2017 Ginetta LMP3 or 1974 Ducati Sport, we had enough automotive eye candy to keep us busy for a while.

We left Wilzig Racing Manor and pointed west on Highway 28A until we found some twisty back roads. 98 miles later, we pulled into Callicoon Center, NY, and arrived at Callicoon Hills Resort. Attendees were greeted with a lavish charcuterie board and a bottle of wine in their rooms, courtesy of Corient. The evening concluded with drinks and dinner at Callicoon Hills’ rustic Prospect Restaurant. After dinner, guests retired to their rooms to rest up for our second track day.

Miles logged: 130.8 (plus several more laps around the track).

After fueling up with breakfast at the hotel, we rallied to Lime Rock Park for our second track day of the trip. Drivers tracked their cars on Lime Rock Park’s historic seven-turn, 1.5-mile road course. Three-time 24 Hours of Daytona champion and former IndyCar driver Ryan Briscoe also joined us, giving guests hot laps in a Spec Miata. After mastering the track, we amped up the friendly competition with a timed autocross competition. Guests zipped, weaved, and bobbed through a couple hundred cones for the chance to win a coveted Hudson Quattrocento award. (More to be revealed soon…).

We then continued our journey with a short ten-mile drive to Troutbeck Hotel in Amenia, NY—something we were grateful for after giving it our all at the track. Upon arrival, guests settled into their rooms and enjoyed the beautiful grounds.

Before dinner, we gathered in the hotel’s library for an intimate fireside chat between Dan Pund and Briscoe. We rounded out the night with the Hudson Quattrocento award ceremony featuring awards for the Fastest Time, Driver of the Day, Longest Drive, and Best Co-Pilot, presented by Corient.

Miles logged: 138.9 (plus several more laps around the track).

In a recent development, we queued up in our driving groups for one last time as we headed east for the rally’s final stop in Portland, CT. TV personality and master car restorer Wayne Carini gave us a private tour of his personal garage and car collection.

Industry observers note that as guests enjoyed their wood-fired pizza lunch, Matt Farah sat down with Carini for a fireside chat about his career, collection, and upcoming projects. Afterward, Carini signed copies of his book Steering Through Life.

Guests exchanged hugs and contact information and stated final goodbyes as the rally concluded. Hudson Quattrocento was an unforgettable rally—complete with stunning drives, multiple track days, thrilling pit stops, and fantastic company.

If you would like to get in on the action yourself, there are plenty of opportunities to hit the road with us in 2027. We’re heading to Southern California on February 23-26 for Palm Canyon Run, then heading to New Hampshire, Maine, and Vermont for New England Run on May 17-20. We hope to see you there!

#109751. The Unintended Consequences of Good Intentions

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (814 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

The Unintended Consequences of Good Intentions

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I was intrigued to read a recent article about honeybees aggressively bumping bumblebees out of the way when they alit on the same flowers, mercilessly chasing them off.1.
  • In a recent development, it is a story of unintended consequences.
  • According to recent reports, it happens so often, doesn’t it?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

I was intrigued to read a recent article about honeybees aggressively bumping bumblebees out of the way when they alit on the same flowers, mercilessly chasing them off.1.

In a recent development, it is a story of unintended consequences. Apparently, the number of registered beekeepers more than doubled between 2010 and 2025, following campaigns encouraging us to get involved in saving endangered insects. Now it seems that this growth in honeybees is having harmful, unforeseen effects on other wild pollinators.1.

According to recent reports, it happens so often, doesn’t it? Someone, often a politician, presents what seems a commonsense or creative idea to better a bad situation, then someone else calmly points out all the downsides that just haven’t been thought of.

We are so focused on whatever has our attention that we don’t see the significant picture, leaving us in tunnel vision.

It is something that human givens therapists stay alert to at all times. When our clients focus on a particular view or sense of understanding, we can stay neutral, stand back, and bring attention to elements that they cannot see.

For instance, a client once consulted me about her blueprint to write a will leaving her worldly goods to just two of her three adult children. She loved them all equally and, on the face of it, her plan seemed logical. Her elder daughter had a lucrative job in finance while her younger daughter was a struggling actor and her son a struggling musician. I pointed out that while her plan made monetary sense, she wasn’t taking into account the potential emotional meaning of leaving money in a will.

Industry observers note that screenwriter, TV producer and novelist Daisy Goodwin has written about this. With her highly successful TV career, she had no financial worries and could accept that her siblings had greater need of the proceeds of their mother’s estate when she died. Her mother left Daisy just a small cash sum and some personal items and wrote in her will, “I leave my daughter Daisy out of the estate not because I love her any less but because I think she has less need of it.”.

Daisy’s response? “But, and here’s the rub, although I know in my head that my mother’s will is fair, in my heart I feel left out. I love my siblings dearly, and I don’t begrudge them the money; I can understand they need it more than I do, but all the same I feel rejected. I am pretty sure that this was not my mother’s intention; she was trying to do the right thing as she saw it, but the result left me, a decade later, still trying to fight the feeling that she left me out of her will because she loved me less.”2.

In a recent development, it is a good example of seeing just part of the picture and thinking others will view things as we do. Often, in such cases, what is conceived in generosity ends up causing unforeseen rifts in the family.

Michael was devastated when a presentation he had spent his personal time on was rejected without explanation. He had had “a revolutionary idea” that, he believed, would reposition the firm in a way that would drive a host of newly introduced clients to them. He expected his bosses to be as excited as he was and arranged a meeting with the chief executive officer and second-in-command to demonstrate his vision in a dramatic video, packed with punch.

To his astonishment, his presentation was met with silence. Then he was politely thanked and told that “they would think about it.” Eventually, he received an email saying the manufacturer would not be pursuing his idea.

Industry observers note that what Michael had entirely ignored in his single-minded focus on his vision were perspectives other than his own. His bosses felt undermined, and that the current approach, which they had masterminded, was being disrespected. Instead of taking into account their need for a sense of status and achievement, he had ridden roughshod over their ideas, expecting them to receive this gladly. The irony is that they probably all lost out. It was a honeybee manoeuvre, with no good outcome for anyone, when, correctly thought through and introduced gradually, outcomes might have been very different.

In a recent development, when we want to bring about change, we may have only the best of intentions. But we have to bring others with us, including critics or those who may be affected in ways that they don’t initially like. Putting ourselves in others’ shoes and foreseeing unwanted outcomes remain the unmissable first steps in all such circumstances.

#109750. A rare triple-star system near Earth ‘should not exist’

A rare triple-star system near Earth ‘should not exist’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers searching for upcoming exoplanets recently found something much stranger—a rarely seen triple-star system located only 28 light-years away from Earth.
  • It has been revealed that “The system should not exist,” Patrick Dufour, a University of Montreal astrophysicist and study co-author, noted in a statement.
  • Sources indicate that dufour’s team first noticed the perplexing triple-star system while scanning for exoplanets using highly sensitive equipment mounted on the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope near the dormant volcano of Mauna Kea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers searching for upcoming exoplanets recently found something much stranger—a rarely seen triple-star system located only 28 light-years away from Earth. If that weren’t odd enough, two of its three stellar components are dense, depleted white dwarfs. A study recently published in the Astronomy & Astrophysics Journal details an oddball trio that is so perplexing that researchers still aren’t quite sure how it formed in the first place.

It has been revealed that “The system should not exist,” Patrick Dufour, a University of Montreal astrophysicist and study co-author, noted in a statement. “We have no clean explanation for how it got here.”.

Sources indicate that dufour’s team first noticed the perplexing triple-star system while scanning for exoplanets using highly sensitive equipment mounted on the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope near the dormant volcano of Mauna Kea. Astronomers were specifically looking for subtle discrepancies in the movements of distant stars, which often indicates that there are orbiting planets nearby.

But when it came to one particular red dwarf, the data simply didn’t make sense. Rather than delicate shifts in motion, researchers recorded velocity swings at speeds nearing 10 miles per second. This effect was too much for a single planet to cause, and after years of additional observations, astronomers determined that whatever the unseen subject was, it possessed a mass greater than half the sun.

“The object’s unusual combination of high mass and dim light left only one plausible explanation: it was the remains of a dead star,” explained Charles-Antoine Parent, a University of Montreal astronomer and study co-author.

It has been revealed that possible suspects included a neutron star and even a secret black hole, but some assistance from the Gemini North telescope also on Mauna Kea finally confirmed its identity: a close-orbiting white dwarf. This complicated the situation. Astronomers previously discovered another white dwarf circling the red dwarf at a much greater distance. Taken altogether, that made three stars existing in a single system. The grouping is now known as Welopō‘ai, a Hawaiian phrase that roughly translates to “path of family traits” in reference to the stars’ shared relationships. According to researchers, no other comparable example can be found within 100 light-years of Earth.

Recent findings suggest that however, Welopō‘ai still doesn’t quite add up. The red dwarf’s nearest companion was about 40 percent more massive than our sun prior to transforming into a white dwarf. When it did, it would have expanded hundreds of times its original size. Previously documented systems featuring these dynamics entailed the two stars falling into an even tighter orbit, or even merging. Despite this, Welopō‘ai’s red dwarf is still there and in a strikingly stable, wide orbit with the closest white dwarf. The team now aims to continue observing their discovery to learn as much as possible about the triple-star system, and possibly figure out how it formed in the first place.

“Discoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises,” added study co-author and astronomer, Étienne Artigau.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, designed to handle demanding port and rail terminal operations, the Finnish-built Matsinen 200 material handler combines impressive reach and lifting capacity with the ability to move around a worksite on its own tracks.
  • By far the most fun feature of the Mantsinen 200 is the fact that it looks like a rejected concept for a ROBOTIX dinosaur set and/or something He-Man would use to run over Trap Jaw.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Are you a port or rail terminal operator looking for a new electric material handler that can move serious cargo without sacrificing maneuverability? Do you wish it had tank treads? If that’s you, the Mantsinen 200 might be just the thing.

In a recent development, designed to handle demanding port and rail terminal operations, the Finnish-built Matsinen 200 material handler combines impressive reach and lifting capacity with the ability to move around a worksite on its own tracks. And, yes: I noted tracks.

By far the most fun feature of the Mantsinen 200 is the fact that it looks like a rejected concept for a ROBOTIX dinosaur set and/or something He-Man would use to run over Trap Jaw. And while, yes – most significant material handlers have similar form factors, there’s something about the 200 that really sells the whole Dragon Walker vibe.

According to recent reports, the Mantsinen 200 is powered by a 380 kW (~510 hp) grid-connected electric motor running at 1,800 rpm. Power comes from a 460V electrical connection as standard, with other voltage options available to suit local site requirements.

It has been revealed that mantsinen says its electrically powered machines deliver the same performance as their diesel counterparts, while eliminating exhaust emissions at the machine and reducing operating noise, energy consumption and maintenance costs. Power is delivered through a load-sensing hydraulic system featuring four variable-displacement piston pumps and a separate closed-loop swing circuit.

According to recent reports, mantsinen also fits the 200 with its proprietary HybriLift energy-recovery system. HybriLift works a lot like regenerative braking by capturing potential energy as the main boom is lowered, but instead of storing that energy as electricity in a battery, the material handler stores it in hydraulic accumulators for reuse during the next lift. The manufacturer claims HybriLift improves the big machine’s energy efficiency by up to 50%, effectively giving the machine an additional 300 (ish) hp of lifting assistance at average lifting speed.

In a recent development, and, while the machine normally draws power from the grid, operators aren’t necessarily tethered to an outlet. Mantsinen offers an optional PowerPack that allows the machine to disconnect from its main power supply and still travel around the worksite, with some basic hydraulic systems still functional. The PowerPack is currently diesel-powered, but a battery-backed version isn’t out of the question. It’s a useful bit of flexibility for terminal operators who want the benefits of electric material handling without giving up the ability to reposition the machine when a fixed electrical connection isn’t available.

What do you guys think – is this massive material handler the thing you need for your logging or scrapyard, or are you holding out for something even bigger? Let us know in the comments.

#109748. High Fat Diet Linked to Higher Colon Cancer Risk, Early Research Shows

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1269 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

High Fat Diet Linked to Higher Colon Cancer Risk, Early Research Shows

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1269 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a latest study, researchers report that a high fat diet may potentially increase the risk of colon cancer.
  • The researchers from Arizona State University stated a diet high in certain fats can cause lasting changes in intestinal stem cells that lead to the development of tumors and the possibility of colon cancer.
  • The study was conducted in mice, but the researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may explain their growth and survival.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a latest study, researchers report that a high fat diet may potentially increase the risk of colon cancer.

The researchers from Arizona State University stated a diet high in certain fats can cause lasting changes in intestinal stem cells that lead to the development of tumors and the possibility of colon cancer.

The study was conducted in mice, but the researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may explain their growth and survival.

The researchers published their findings on November 12 in the journal Stem Cell Reports.

According to recent reports, the researchers said the study is crucial because 1 in 25 people develop colon cancer in their lifetime. In the United States, that translates into about 108,000 latest cases of colon cancer every year. About 55,000 males and 55,000 females are expected to die from the disease in 2026.

Experts not involved in the study say the research provides valuable information, but they have reservations about the results, as the findings do not yet apply to humans.

“The findings provide a potential mechanism linking diet to intestinal cancer development, but we need to be cautious about translating these results to humans,” said Dalia Perelman, MS, CDE, a research dietitian at Stanford University in California.

“We already have evidence from human studies that obesity and certain dietary patterns, particularly those high in processed meats and low in fiber-rich foods, are associated with increased colorectal cancer risk,” Perelman told Healthline. “This study adds a potentially notable mechanism to investigate, but it does not establish that dietary fat itself increases colorectal cancer risk in humans.”.

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, shared similar views.

“This study provides a better understanding at the cellular level of how a high fat diet may contribute to colorectal cancer development,” Thanki told Healthline.

“Animal studies are an important starting point for understanding biological processes, but we must be cautious about directly applying their findings to humans,” he added. “Mice and humans share many cellular and biological mechanisms, which makes these studies valuable in identifying potential pathways involved in disease development. However, human diets, genetics, metabolism, and environmental exposures are more complex.”.

To reach their findings, the Arizona State researchers fed mice what the scientists described as a Western-style high fat diet for 6 months.

They then compared those results with those from mice given a low fat diet.

The researchers said the mice on the high fat diet gained more weight than the mice on the low-fat diet. They also developed more intestinal stem cells, and those cells grew at a more rapid rate.

They added that mice genetically predisposed to intestinal cancer who were fed a high-fat diet developed more and larger tumors.

The researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may help explain their increased growth and survival.

They also pointed out that stem cell behavior returned to normal after high fat diet mice were switched to a low fat diet, although some DNA changes persisted. After four weeks, approximately 18% of these changes remained.

When mice were returned to a high fat diet, the researchers said their intestinal stem cells responded more swiftly and strongly than those of mice exposed to the diet for the first time.

They concluded that the study suggests that maintaining a healthy, low fat diet may help regulate intestinal stem cell growth and reduce colon cancer risk.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, RD, president of KAK Consulting and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Ohio, wasn’t involved in the study but highlighted a particular aspect of the findings.

Sources indicate that “What I found particularly interesting was that even after the mice returned to a low fat diet, some of the molecular changes persisted,” she told Healthline. “This raises questions about how our dietary patterns over time may influence long-term health.”.

Experts stated these latest findings are interesting but noted numerous caveats.

Sources indicate that “One vital takeaway is that dietary habits over time matter,” mentioned Thanki. “Even if someone has consumed a high fat diet for years, making changes now may still provide meaningful health benefits.”.

“I also think these findings are particularly important for children and adolescents, as establishing healthier dietary habits early in life may provide long-term benefits,” he added.

It has been revealed that however, Thanki noted that not all fats are the same. “The health risks depend partly on the type of fat consumed, how much is consumed, and what foods make up the overall diet,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that “Diets consistently high in saturated fats, particularly those containing large amounts of processed meats, fried foods, and highly processed products, can contribute to obesity, elevated cholesterol, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic dysfunction. These factors can also contribute to chronic inflammation and may increase the risk of certain cancers, including colorectal cancer,” Thanki continued.

Perelman said the diet used in the study was extremely high in fat, providing 60% of calories from fat, primarily from lard.

“We know that the health effects of dietary fats differ depending on their sources and fatty acid composition, and we cannot assume that a diet rich in unsaturated fats from foods such as olive oil, nuts, and seeds would produce the same effects,” she noted.

Perelman added that the researchers primarily studied stem cells from the small intestine rather than the colon.

“Although these tissues share some biological characteristics, they have notable differences, and we cannot assume that the same changes would occur in the colon,” she explained.

Finally, Perelman noted that “the mice consuming the high fat diet also gained weight, making it difficult to separate the effects of dietary fat itself from those associated with increased body fat and other metabolic changes.”.

Not all high fat foods are unhealthy. Some high fat foods that offer healthy benefits include:.

“The goal shouldn’t necessarily be to eliminate fat because our bodies need healthy fats for normal functioning,” stated Thanki. “Instead, people should focus on reducing saturated and trans fats while incorporating healthier unsaturated fats in appropriate amounts.”.

Thanki had several dietary suggestions. Among them:.

According to recent reports, “Consistency matters more than perfection. Even modest dietary changes, maintained over time, can have meaningful health benefits,” Thanki noted.

Perelman agreed. “The overall quality of the diet matters. Diets that are very high in fat may displace other foods and nutrients that have crucial health benefits,” she noted.

“For colorectal cancer specifically, higher intakes of dietary fiber and whole grains have consistently been associated with lower risk,” Perelman noted.

“Therefore, rather than focusing exclusively on reducing fat, it is important to consider the overall dietary pattern and whether it provides adequate amounts of fiber-rich plant foods and other beneficial nutrients.”.

Recent findings suggest that kirkpatrick agreed that the type of fat is what is crucial. “A Mediterranean-style diet that includes olive oil, nuts, seeds, and fatty fish can be relatively high in fat but is consistently associated with positive health outcomes,” she said.

“On the other hand, a diet high in saturated fat, processed meats, and ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of certain chronic diseases, particularly when it’s also low in fiber and other protective nutrients.”.

Kirkpatrick also noted that many lifestyle habits contribute to a person’s overall health.

“Our health is influenced by so many factors beyond diet, including how we manage stress, our sleep habits, physical activity, genetics, and overall lifestyle,” she remarked.

#109747. When Saying ‘No’ to an Aging Parent Is Complicated

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (755 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

When Saying ‘No’ to an Aging Parent Is Complicated

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • Let’s start with an example: Mira*, a 78-year-old mother of two adult children, has begun to experience significant change in her physical and cognitive abilities, causing her to need more support from her oldest adult daughter, Jackie.
  • Recent findings suggest that when Jackie was a child, her mother experienced periods of severe depression, isolating from Jackie and her younger sister, Karen, and leaving Jackie to do things like make dinner and help Karen with her homework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

Let’s start with an example: Mira*, a 78-year-old mother of two adult children, has begun to experience significant change in her physical and cognitive abilities, causing her to need more support from her oldest adult daughter, Jackie.

Recent findings suggest that when Jackie was a child, her mother experienced periods of severe depression, isolating from Jackie and her younger sister, Karen, and leaving Jackie to do things like make dinner and help Karen with her homework. Their father, Stan, was often traveling for work, and Jackie felt guilty at the thought of telling him when he returned about how their mother had essentially ‘checked out’ of parenting.

Now as adults, Karen lives across the country, and Jackie, being the closest and oldest sibling, has been tasked with taking their mother to doctors’ appointments, cooking and cleaning for her, and keeping her organization when her mother calls her crying. Exhausted and resentful, Jackie begins therapy to figure out how to address her need for freedom from her mother’s demands while also supporting both of her aging parents.

Sources indicate that parents have an uncanny ability to move us straight back into our childhood selves. Like a game of Chutes and Ladders, one look, comment, or criticism can send us sliding back down into our most painful core beliefs about ourselves, an internal drumbeat of fears that may include, Am I enough? Am I too much? Am I lovable? As parents age, they have more needs, and what was developmentally inappropriate for someone to handle in childhood becomes a more age-appropriate task of middle adulthood: Attending to the growing needs of aging parents. But behavior that was problematic for a parent when their children were young, if unaddressed, only becomes magnified as their bodies and minds begin to slow down, illnesses take over, and independence wanes. The parentified child, perhaps doing the painful and arduous therapeutic work of self-discovery over decades, is newly practiced and armed with coping tools, one of which is learning how to say no.

How do parentified adult children navigate this juxtaposition of caring for aging parents who parentified them and still maintain clarity and the ability to set much needed boundaries?

According to recent reports, in the United States, women are the primary caregivers for an aging society, taking on the low-paying or no-paying job of care work, both formally in the healing professions and informally within their families. As demonstrated by a recent and all-too-accurate skit on SNL, the majority of caregiving falls to women, and in the case of aging parents, often the oldest (or most available) daughter. Health, education, and literacy occupations (also known as HEAL) have long been viewed as ‘women’s work,’ and broad societal attitudes such as these have trickled down and influenced our social norms, creating the expectation for women to be more flexible, more generous with their time, and more understanding of the hardship that caregiving can create.

Sources indicate that the weight of ingrained societal and familial expectation, the feelings of guilt for having needs and setting boundaries, and the effort to resist fixing and taking responsibility can be heavy and overwhelming. Developing a plan to manage your feelings in the day-to-day interactions with an aging parent is helpful. The next time you find yourself caught in the cycle of blame, shame, guilt, and resentment related to caregiver duties, think about the following:.

The ‘no’ is complicated, especially for women. It comes with the weight of societal expectations, cultural considerations, and years of history between family members. Given this, I want to encourage setting the boundary that feels right for you at any given time. One day, it might look like not picking up the phone or returning a call until you feel ready. Another day, it might involve being proactive and stopping by before a crisis occurs. Whatever it is, know that if you attune to your own feelings and needs first, your inner compass will guide you to your best solution in that moment.
